Q: Variational Autoencoders Visualisation A:

I was checking whether visual explainability had been investigated for VAEs and found the workaround below, including an archived paper: "VAE Explainer: Supplement Learning Variational Autoencoders with Interactive Visualization". Authors offered an interactive visualization for latent space: https://xnought.github.io/vae-explainer/

This could address your question.

"...am unable to figure out how this would all translate visually, like what is the purpose of P(z) (=> the latent space distribution) and what it would do intuitively.."

Note 1: I was looking at VAE as well as "What are the roles of the prior p(z) in a VAE?", and if you want to focus on latent space distribution, it's denoted by Z as the latent vector and Probabilistic Modeling for encoder & decoder denoted with q_ϕ(z∣x) & p_θ(z∣x) respectively. see this post:

Note 2: According to this post, AE has one latent vector while VAE has multiple latent vectors.

Q: ZeroMQ subscriber in Rails worker fails to receive messages A:

I needed to set ZAP_DOMAIN too. In the Quake Live server logs, for the username, you see stats_stats. It's concatenating the domain to the username with _, so the username is stats and the domain is stats. A working version of a Ruby on Rails listener:

require 'ffi-rzmq'
require 'json'

# Define constants for ZMQ connection
ZMQ_USERNAME = 'stats'.b # this is the default username, AFAIK you cannot change it
ZMQ_PASSWORD = 'XXXX'.b
ZMQ_HOST = < add your server IP >
ZMQ_PORT = '27960' # change to the right port in case
ZMQ_URL = "tcp://#{ZMQ_HOST}:#{ZMQ_PORT}"
ZAP_DOMAIN = 'stats'.b  # Explicit ZAP domain

begin
  # Create ZMQ context and subscriber socket
  context = ZMQ::Context.new
  subscriber = context.socket(ZMQ::SUB)

  # Set authentication credentials
  if ZMQ_USERNAME && ZMQ_PASSWORD
    subscriber.setsockopt(ZMQ::PLAIN_USERNAME, ZMQ_USERNAME)
    subscriber.setsockopt(ZMQ::PLAIN_PASSWORD, ZMQ_PASSWORD)
    puts "Authentication credentials set. Username: #{ZMQ_USERNAME}, Password: #{ZMQ_PASSWORD}"
  else
    puts "No authentication credentials provided."
  end

  # Set the ZAP domain
  subscriber.setsockopt(ZMQ::ZAP_DOMAIN, ZAP_DOMAIN)
  puts "ZAP domain set to: #{ZAP_DOMAIN}"

  # Connect to ZMQ server
  subscriber.connect(ZMQ_URL)
  puts "Connecting to ZeroMQ PUB socket at: #{ZMQ_URL}"

  # Subscribe to all messages
  subscriber.setsockopt(ZMQ::SUBSCRIBE, '')
  puts "Subscribed to ZeroMQ PUB socket, listening for all events."

  # Listen for messages
  loop do
    message = ''
    begin
      subscriber.recv_string(message)
      puts "Received message: #{message}"
    rescue ZMQ::Error => e
      puts "ZeroMQ error: #{e.message}"
      break
    rescue => e
      puts "Error receiving message: #{e.message}"
      break
    end
  end
rescue => e
  puts "Fatal error: #{e.message}"
ensure
  subscriber&.close
  context&.terminate
  puts "ZeroMQ subscriber stopped."
end

Q: Compiling Quake 3 Arena on Xcode 16 fails due to the version of the Xcode project A:

To elaborate on the "just use ioquake3" comments, you have to consider the history of the codebase and what your intent is.

Quake 3 shipped in 1999 and the Mac version originally ran on Mac OS 8 (aka "Classic Mac OS") on PowerPC Macs. Mac OS X support was patched in later. The code delivered as open source in 2005 doesn't even really have an Xcode project, the pbproj included is for Project Builder, an Xcode predecessor.

In the two decades since (the code release is 20 years old, it was only added to GitHub 14 years ago - GitHub itself being only 17 years old), source port projects have done the work to get the code building on more modern systems. That said, I can understand the urge to want to get in and tinker with the original from a retrocomputing hobbyist angle.

So if your intention is to see if you can personally get the original 2005 source code building on a modern Mac, I would suggest creating a new Xcode project and importing the files into it and getting them building that way. You'll likely run into a number of issues with deprecated things, many of which are solved by modern source ports, but those are the messy bits you can work through. You could also pursue writing a Makefile if Make is more your style.

If your intention is to see if you can get the code running on a more period-appropriate Mac you can either find an old Mac or emulate one via UTM, even on Apple Silicon. This will be its own journey as you'll need to hunt down all the old development software but there's entire websites dedicated to preserving this stuff.

If your intention is just to get the engine up and running then yeah a more modern source port like ioquake3 or quake3e (which I believe still has the option to run sans-SDL, like the old one would) will get you to the goal quicker.

Q: How to structure a React project for stock management? A:
  • Sorting React components into "components" and "pages is pretty typical.
  • Instead of "redux" one might call this directory "state"
  • A "services", or sometimes "api", directory makes sense.

It's unclear what the "features" directory would be though. Also, if are using Redux-Toolkit then it's likely you are also, or ought to be, using Redux-Toolkit Query for your API/service calls. And in this case you'd likely merge the "redux"/"state" and "services"/"api" directories since RTK/Q would handle the entire Redux store including the API slices.

What is the best folder structure for this kind of project?

There is no one single "best..." for this, or generally any programming problem. Many solutions work great for most problems, but there is hardly any "one-size-fits-all" in existence.

Should I separate features (product, variant, stock) or use pages/components only?

My advice here would be to place all general-purpose UI components into the "components" directory. These are your building blocks, i.e. units of UI code, that are used to compose larger and more complex UI components, all the way up to what you may consider page/container components. Either use a completely flat structure here, or use a grouping structure that makes sense to you, your team, or whatever is easiest in the specific project repo.

  • Flat component tree

    src/components/
  - header.tsx
  - footer.tsx
  - spinner.tsx
  - orderedList.tsx
  ...

  • Grouped component tree

    src/components/
  - layout/
    - header.tsx
    - footer.tsx
  - common/
    - spinner.tsx
    - text.tsx
  - forms/
    - textInput.tsx
    - passwordInput.tsx
  ...

The page/container components could be your fully-fledged pages that handle/marry your UI to your services, i.e. handles UI lifecycle, initiates data requests, etc.

How do professionals usually organize similar projects?

Probably similar to what I've described above. To get a good overview how production code is organized across a broad spectrum you should take a look at the source code of popular libraries and dependencies you are using, like the Redux (core), React-Redux, and Redux-Toolkit libraries, Material-UI/MUI, etc.

Q: Macro Modification A:

If "TimeEntries_2026_04_15-2026_04_" is where your're adding the formulas:

Sub PenaltyNew()
    
    Dim ws As Worksheet, lastRow As Long
    
    Set ws = ActiveSheet 'or some other specific sheet
    'find the last row:choose a column which always has data
    lastRow = ws.Cells(ws.Rows.Count, "A").End(xlUp).Row
    
    ws.Range("T2:T" & lastRow).Formula2R1C1 = _
                    "=LOOKUP(2,1/(R2C[-19]:RC[-19]<>""""),ROW(R2C[-19]:RC[-19]))"
    
    ws.Range("U2:U" & lastRow).Formula2R1C1 = _
                    "=AND(ISNUMBER(SEARCH(""MISSED BREAK"",UPPER(TRIM(INDEX(C3,RC20)))))," & _
                          "OR(UPPER(TRIM(RC18))=""MISSED"",RC18=0))"
    
    ws.Name = "Sheet1"                'rename the sheet
    Set ws = Sheets.Add(After:=ws)    'add new sheet and get a reference to it
    ws.Range("A1").Formula2R1C1 = "=[your very long formula here]"
    ws.Select

End Sub

Q: Should a destructor delete pointer members of the class? A:

Should MyClass have a destructor which uses something like delete MyPtr?

If MyClass owns the memory that MyPtr points at, then yes, MyClass will need to delete that memory at some point during its lifetime, such as in the destructor. This is best handled using smart pointers like std::unique_ptr or std::shared_ptr to manage the memory cleanup for you. Stay away from using new and delete manually, if you can help it.

On the other hand, if the memory that MyPtr is pointing at was allocated and is owned elsewhere, and MyClass is just holding a pointer to that memory, then delete MyPtr is not needed.

Or, is MyPtr destroyed when I call delete my?

new MyClass allocates sizeof(MyClass) bytes of memory for a new MyClass object, and then calls the MyClass constructor on that memory to initialize its data. Conversely, delete my calls the ~MyClass() destructor on the object's memory to finalize its data, and then frees the memory that new allocated.

So, the MyPtr data member itself is destroyed during MyClass's destruction, yes. But, the memory that MyPtr is pointing at is not destroyed, unless the destructor does so explicitly (or if the memory is managed by a smart pointer that frees the memory when the pointer itself is destructed).
